claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, and 9, run a zero-training internal-readout study on an open safety-aligned model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, or Mistral-7B-Instruct using public harmful/safe prompt sets from HarmBench, JailbreakBench, and AdvBench plus benign prompts from Alpaca or WildChat. First identify genuinely successful jailbreak cases using a public judge such as the HarmBench classifier or Llama Guard. For each plain harmful prompt, successful jailbreak version, failed jailbreak version, and benign prompt, record residual-stream and attention-head outputs. Define a pre-registered no-training detector by applying the model’s own unembedding or logit-lens projection to internal activations and scoring fixed verbalizers such as unsafe versus safe, harmful versus harmless, or refusal-related versus compliance-related tokens; do not fit any probe or threshold on labels, and report AUROC/AUPRC. Compare this detector to dedicated public safety models such as Llama Guard, WildGuard, and the HarmBench classifier. If harmful-input information remains linearly/logit-lens readable in successful jailbreaks at similar levels to plain harmful prompts, that supports persistence rather than elimination; if the readout collapses specifically on successful jailbreaks, that supports elimination or representational rewriting. If the zero-training detector is competitive with dedicated safety models, that supports the direct-readout/no-additional-training subclaims; if it only works after fitting a probe or is much worse than safety models, those subclaims weaken. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a released benchmark with cached activations for successful jailbreaks, a fully specified zero-training readout, and head/layer-wise detector metrics against the same dedicated safety baselines.

With respect to evidence piece 2 from The Struggle Between Continuation and Refusal, replicate and extend the head-level causal intervention analysis to test subclaims 3, 4, and 5. On the same public HarmBench/JailbreakBench/AdvBench prompts, find attention heads whose activations differ most between refused plain harmful prompts and successful jailbreak prompts, then use activation/path patching and zero-ablation during generation. Prioritize heads where restoring the plain-harmful activation into a jailbreak increases refusal, and where zeroing the head on a plain harmful prompt increases attack success rate. Quantify whether the implicated set is small, for example less than 1 to 5 percent of heads, and compare against random same-size head sets, neighboring heads, MLP ablations, and whole-layer ablations. If successful jailbreaks consistently suppress a compact set of safety heads and zeroing only those heads turns many refusals into harmful compliance while random controls do not, the selective-bypass mechanism is supported. If many heads are required, the heads are not suppressed during jailbreaks, or ablation does not increase compliance, the small-subset suppression claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by stronger published evidence reporting head identities, activation changes under successful jailbreaks, causal ablation effects, and random-head controls across multiple models and datasets.

To address subclaim 6, test whether non-suppressed attention heads continue to represent harmful content during successful jailbreaks. Using public HarmBench categories and benign controls, train simple diagnostic probes only on non-jailbroken plain prompts to predict harmful versus benign input, and optionally harmful category, from individual head outputs or small head groups; then evaluate these probes on held-out successful jailbreak prompts. Separately, perform causal sanity checks by ablating or patching the heads with the strongest harmful-content readout while leaving the previously identified safety-head subset untouched, and measure whether harmful-content readout or category evidence changes without merely changing refusal style. If many non-safety heads retain high harmful-content probe accuracy on successful jailbreaks, especially when the safety heads are suppressed, this supports the claim that harmful-content representations persist elsewhere. If harmful-content probes fail specifically on successful jailbreaks or the only readable signals are in the suppressed safety heads, the persistence-in-other-heads subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by existing per-head activation datasets showing robust harmful-category readouts on successful jailbreaks together with causal patching or ablation controls separating content representation from refusal execution.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct within-model comparison of a safety-relevant internal signal on matched unattacked and successfully attacked requests, across the computation, that can distinguish persistence of the signal from its disappearance.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 records internal activations for plain harmful and successful-jailbreak versions and reads them with refusal/compliance and harmful/safe projections, while experiments 1 and 2 add causal evidence about the suppressed and non-suppressed head populations. Together the set can determine whether safety-relevant information remains internally available during successful attacks rather than being globally erased.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A paired collection of harmful requests that are refused without an attack but succeed with an attack, allowing attack effects to be separated from differences in the underlying requests.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiments 0 and 1 explicitly use each plain harmful prompt together with its successful jailbreak version and require genuine successful cases; experiment 2 also trains on plain prompts and evaluates on successful jailbreak prompts. The team would therefore have the paired refused-versus-successful cases needed for the comparison.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A head-level procedure that identifies compact head subsets by their activation and causal roles in refusal and jailbreak behavior, with controls that distinguish those roles from generic effects of perturbing heads.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 discovers heads from refused-versus-successful cases, tests restoration and ablation, quantifies subset size, and includes random, neighboring, MLP, and layer controls. Experiment 2 separately characterizes the remaining heads by harmful-content readout. This provides an alternative, causally grounded way to identify the two relevant head populations; the particular projection, cutoff, and bandwidth calibration are not requirements of the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention showing that suppressing only the implicated small head subset changes a normally refusing model to harmful compliance, with matched perturbation controls.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 directly performs head restoration and zero-ablation during generation, measures attack success, tests whether only a small fraction of heads suffices, and compares random same-size, neighboring, MLP, and whole-layer interventions. This has the needed causal and control structure even though its perturbation need not use the reference's exact feature injection.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A test on successful jailbreak inputs that suppresses the alternative, non-refusal head population and measures whether the persistent harmful-content signal in the rest of the computation is reduced.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 2 trains content readouts on ordinary harmful versus benign inputs, evaluates them on held-out successful jailbreaks, and ablates or patches the strongest non-safety-head readouts while leaving the identified safety-head subset untouched. The readout and causal sanity checks can establish whether other heads continue to carry harmful-content information during attack success.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-level attribution that separately measures head responses to the original harmful request and to the jailbreak template, allowing selective template handling to be distinguished from a generic difference in sensitivity to harmful content.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments compare aggregate head activations, train head-level content probes, and perform head interventions, but none decomposes activation into contributions from original harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment's mechanistic discrimination requires separating each head's contribution from the harmful request from its contribution from the jailbreak template.
Proposed experiments 0-2 do not perform token-level attribution or an equivalent decomposition; their aggregate differences can mix both token sources.
Therefore a head-type difference could still be explained by generic sensitivity to harmful content rather than selective handling of the attack template.
The team would fail to learn whether the proposed bypass mechanism defeats that rival sensitivity explanation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: External validation of a training-free harmful-input readout across diverse models and safety benchmarks, with direct comparison to the model's refusal behavior and dedicated safety detectors to establish transfer and competitive quality.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 does specify a no-training internal readout, quantitative discrimination metrics, and comparison with dedicated safety models, so it can test direct readout and competitiveness. Its stated scope is an open model and a limited set of public prompt resources rather than broad validation across multiple architecture families and many independent safety benchmarks, so a positive result would leave transfer and robustness across safety-aligned LLMs ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference establishes not only that a detector works once, but that the training-free readout transfers across models and diverse safety evaluations while remaining competitive with dedicated detectors.
[2] Proposed experiment 0 tests the same idea with fixed verbalizers and external baselines, but its stated design can be run on only one selected model and a narrower evaluation set.
[3] A positive result there would show usefulness in that setting without showing that the readout generalizes beyond that model or prompt distribution.
[4] A team running the proposed set would fail to learn the broad external transfer and comparative robustness that the reference experiment would have established.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would establish persistence, selective and causally sufficient head suppression, continued harmful-content readout in other heads, and training-free detector quality. It would not, however, resolve the reference experiment's key mechanistic rival: whether the two head populations differ because of jailbreak-template processing rather than because of generic sensitivity to harmful content. That unresolved ambiguity prevents the full selective-bypass claim from being settled.
